--- title: "[GradientBoostingSurvivalAnalysis]{.doc-object-name .doc-class .doc-label .doc-label-class}" body-classes: doc-api-page page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Gradient-boosted survival model minimizing the Cox partial-likelihood loss. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_boosting.py#L195-L428){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.CLASS} ```python GradientBoostingSurvivalAnalysis( *, n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=3, subsample=1.0, max_features=None, random_state=None ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Builds an additive risk score by sequentially fitting shallow squared-error regression trees to the negative gradient of the negative Cox partial log-likelihood (the martingale residuals under the current model) and adding a shrunken version of each tree. The result is a flexible, non-linear generalization of the Cox model: strong predictive performance on structured tabular data, without a global proportional-hazards assumption on individual covariates. A Breslow baseline hazard turns the additive log-risk score into per-subject survival and cumulative-hazard functions. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n_estimators]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[100]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of boosting iterations (trees). [learning_rate]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[0.1]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Shrinkage applied to each tree's contribution. Smaller values need more trees but generalize better. [max_depth]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[3]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum depth of each regression tree (interaction depth). [min_samples_leaf]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[3]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Minimum number of samples in each leaf of a tree. [subsample]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Fraction of the training rows sampled (without replacement) to grow each tree. Values below `1.0` give stochastic gradient boosting. [max_features]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Covariates considered per split: `None` (all, default), `"sqrt"`, `"log2"`, an int, or a float fraction. [random_state]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Seed or `numpy.random.Generator` for subsampling and per-node feature selection. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Fit a gradient-boosted survival model on the bundled `lung` dataset: ::: {#822176ef .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw # Load data and build a right-censored response lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="pandas").dropna(subset=["ph.ecog", "ph.karno"]) y = gw.Surv.right(lung["time"], event=(lung["status"] == 2)) cols = ["age", "sex", "ph.ecog", "ph.karno", "wt.loss"] # Fit the model and score the first five subjects gbm = gw.GradientBoostingSurvivalAnalysis( n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=2, random_state=0 ).fit(y, lung[cols]) gbm.predict(lung[cols])[:5] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` array([1.66691083, 1.09057783, 0.59369757, 1.18981321, 0.58051085]) ``` ::: ::: ## Methods {.doc-methods}
Name Description
fit() Fit the gradient-boosted survival model to a right-censored response.
predict() Predict a risk score, linear predictor, or survival / cumulative-hazard curves.
variable_importance() Impurity-based variable importance (normalized total squared-error reduction).
### [fit()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Fit the gradient-boosted survival model to a right-censored response. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_boosting.py#L284-L356){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python fit(surv, covariates, *, data=None) ``` ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [surv]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Surv]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A right-censored `Surv` response (built with `Surv.right()`). [covariates]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A dataframe, a 2-D array, or a right-hand-side formula string evaluated against `data`. [data]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : DataFrame used to evaluate a formula string. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [self]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The fitted estimator, with cached attributes including `trees_`, `event_times_`, `feature_importances_`, `n_features_in_`, and `feature_names_in_`. ::: ### [predict()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Predict a risk score, linear predictor, or survival / cumulative-hazard curves. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_boosting.py#L364-L415){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python predict(newdata=None, *, type="risk", times=None, format=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} 1. `type="risk"` (default): the relative hazard $\exp(F(x))$, a 1-D array where higher values indicate higher risk. 2. `type="lp"`: the additive log-risk score $F(x)$ (the boosted Cox linear predictor). 3. `type="survival"`: survival $S(t \mid x) = \exp(-H_0(t)\,e^{F(x)})$ at `times`. 4. `type="cumulative_hazard"`: $H(t \mid x) = H_0(t)\,e^{F(x)}$ at `times`. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [newdata]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Covariates to predict for. `None` predicts for the training subjects. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["risk"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : One of `"risk"`, `"lp"`, `"survival"`, or `"cumulative_hazard"`. [times]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Times at which to evaluate curves. Defaults to the training event times. [format]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : DataFrame backend for curve output. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [numpy.ndarray or DataFrame]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A risk / linear-predictor vector, or a curve frame with a `time` column and one column per subject. ::: ### [variable_importance()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Impurity-based variable importance (normalized total squared-error reduction). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_boosting.py#L417-L428){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python variable_importance(*, format=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Each split's reduction in squared error is credited to its covariate and summed across all trees, then normalized to sum to one. Returns a table sorted by importance. :::
